strengths: The evaluation is unusually broad: 5 understanding tasks plus 8 reasoning benchmarks (with explicit OOD splits) across 6 model variants spanning multiple families (Gemma3, LLaVA, Qwen3-VL at 4B–32B), which gives the data-efficiency and generalization claims reasonable empirical grounding.

The comparison design for the alignment study is fair where it matters: the Textual (10K) baseline uses the same 10K table images as DISCO, so the structure–content disentanglement effect is isolated from data-quantity effects; the Textual (97K)/Textual-All baselines further test the 'quality over quantity' claim.

Useful robustness checks beyond the main task: evaluation on non-tabular benchmarks (ScienceQA, CRPE, HallusionBench, TextVQA, Table 4) directly probes the catastrophic-forgetting concern that motivates the work, and ablations (w/o TL, –GSE, –SSE, only Table-GLS, CoT vs. Table-GLS) map the contribution of each component.

The core idea—decoupling structure learning (anonymized cell contents) from semantic grounding (global/local content alignment)—is simple, clearly described, and plausibly explains the observed data efficiency; training data construction (Appendix B) and prompts (Appendix C) are disclosed in enough detail to reimplement.
The Limitations section is honest and specific (dependence on decoupled data, extra token generation for Table-GLS, table-centric scope).
weaknesses: Novelty is modest. Structure alignment via content anonymization is a lightweight data-construction trick, and the 'local content alignment' (cell lookup at row m, column n) is essentially cell-level grounding similar to Table-LLaVA; Table-GLS is a three-stage prompt-decomposed inference pipeline closely resembling existing decompose-then-verify CoT schemes. Neither component involves a genuinely new training objective—the 'objectives' in Eqs. (2)–(4) are standard NLL losses over differently constructed targets.

Results are mixed in ways the text overstates. The claim that DISCO 'consistently enhances table understanding across all evaluated LVLMs and tasks' is contradicted by the tables: e.g., Qwen3-VL-4B TSD Row drops from 28.70 (None) to 21.70, Gemma3n-E4B RCE Row drops from 8.50 to 4.66, and several OOD cells regress. A more careful, nuanced analysis of when disentanglement helps vs. hurts is needed to support the central claim.

Potential train–test table leakage is not addressed. DISCO alignment samples 10K table images from the MMTab pre-training corpus (Table 5 includes WTQ, HiTab, TAT-QA, TabFact, InfoTabs, etc.), and the understanding evaluation (TCE/TCL/TSD on 1000 tables) is drawn from the same corpus. Even without QA annotations, aligning on the very tables later used for cell-extraction and size-detection evaluation inflates apparent understanding gains, and the paper provides no de-duplication analysis.

Reasoning comparisons against 'optimized LVLMs' are across different backbones (Table-R1 on Qwen2-VL-7B, HIPPO on MiniCPM-V2.6) and taken from original papers, making the 'comparable performance with minimal supervision' claim loose; no significance testing or seed variance is reported anywhere, so many of the smaller margins (often <2 points) may not be meaningful.

The case study (Figure 5) is internally inconsistent and undermines interpretability claims: the non-DISCO Table-GLS run shows sub-table 'Row 5 Column 3: W 17–10' yet reasons over 'W 35–17'; the ground truth is stated as 7 for a game the sample table shows as a loss ('L 17–10'), yet the DISCO variant concludes 'they won the game by 7 points'. These contradictions suggest the case may be partly fabricated or carelessly assembled.

Table-GLS token overhead is substantial (avg 439–492 tokens vs. 241 for CoT in Table 10, roughly 2x), which weakens the 'efficient/lightweight' framing relative to tool-augmented methods; the efficiency trade-off is acknowledged in Limitations but not confronted in the abstract/introduction claims.

Reproducibility artifacts are incomplete: footnote 1 promises 'Our data and code are available at' with no URL, and writing quality is below bar (recurring typos: 'strcuture', 'dection', 'exist methods', 'optimizated', 'focuse'), which for a main-track submission suggests insufficient polish.

strengths: The evaluation is unusually broad: 21 understanding/reasoning tasks across MMTab, multiple LVLM backbones (Gemma3, LLaVA, Qwen3-VL up to 32B), OOD splits, and non-tabular general-capability checks (Table 4), which lends credibility to the data-efficiency claim (10K vs. 97K alignment images).

The disentangled structure–content alignment idea is intuitive and potentially useful: supervising structure via anonymized cell contents is a simple but sensible reframing of table alignment, and the w/o TL ablation supports that structure-only alignment alone brings gains.
Table-GLS is training- and tool-free, and the ablations (–GSE, –SSE, only-Table-GLS, vs. CoT) systematically probe each inference stage rather than presenting only the full system.

Hyperparameters, prompts, and dataset statistics are provided in the appendix, and the limitations section honestly notes dependence on decoupled supervision, added inference latency, and the table-centric scope.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. DISCO reduces to a data-curation choice (anonymize cell values in HTML/Markdown/LaTeX) plus standard LoRA fine-tuning, and Table-GLS is a three-stage prompting pipeline (plan → extract → answer). Both are reasonable engineering contributions but thin for an ICML main-track methods paper; no new architecture, training objective, or theory is introduced.

The central claim of 'consistent' improvement is overstated by the paper's own tables. DISCO regresses sharply on Qwen3-VL-4B TSD (36.60 → 21.70 vs. Textual) and TabMCQ; Gemma3n-E4B DISCO shows mixed results (e.g., RCE Row drops from 19.70 to 4.66, OOD TCL from 12.32 to 6.86); and Table-GLS removes SSE *improves* HiTab. There are no significance tests, seed variance, or confidence intervals, and OOD splits contain only 250 samples, making several claimed gains fragile.

The 'efficiency' framing is not well supported. Table 10 shows Table-GLS roughly doubles generated tokens versus CoT (439 vs. 241 average), yet the abstract and title emphasize efficiency; the discussion only concedes this obliquely. Table 10's caption is also a copy-paste error from Table 9, which undermines confidence in the analysis.

Comparisons with optimized LVLMs (Table-R1 on Qwen2-VL-7B, HIPPO on MiniCPM-V-2.6) cross different backbones and training regimes, so claims of 'matching or surpassing optimized LVLM' are not apples-to-apples; some baselines are quoted from original papers with different prompts and evaluation scripts (only partially remedied for HIPPO).

The case study (Figure 5) contains confusing/erroneous content: the non-DISCO Table-GLS panel shows a sub-table of 'W 17–10' while the reasoning quotes 'W 35–17', and row targeting flips between 'Week 5' and 'Row 5' between conditions, making the motivating example hard to trust as evidence of interpretability.

Substantial writing and presentation sloppiness throughout: missing URL in footnote 1, 'As shown in Figure' without a number, typos ('strucuture', 'focuse', 'exist methods', 'step-step', 'Contruction', 'statitiscs', 'evalute'), and an 'Impact Statements' section that is essentially boilerplate. These suggest the manuscript was not carefully polished.

Key design questions are unexamined: why structure and content objectives must be staged rather than mixed with weighting; how sensitive results are to the anonymization placeholder; whether gains stem from the disentanglement or simply from cell-lookup-style training data that closely mirrors the TCE/TCL/RCE evaluation tasks (a potential task-alignment confound that would inflate the understanding results).

strengths: The paper is well-motivated: separating structural abstraction from semantic grounding during alignment is a clean, interpretable design principle, and the structure alignment via anonymized representations (Eq. 1-2) is a simple but sensible way to force layout learning without cell semantics.

The evaluation breadth is impressive: 21 tasks/benchmarks spanning table understanding (TSD, TCE, TCL, MCD, RCE) and reasoning (5 QA + 3 fact-verification benchmarks), with four backbone LVLMs of different scales/families (Gemma3, Gemma3n, LLaVA-v1.6, Qwen3-VL) plus OOD splits and non-tabular tasks (Table 4) to check for capability regression.

The data-efficiency claim is well supported: DISCO with 10K images matches or beats Textual-All (97K/150K) on most understanding tasks (e.g., Qwen3-VL-8B RCE 55.95 vs 41.42), and the ablation of alignment components (w/o TL) and reasoning stages (-GSE, -SSE) is informative, including the honest observation that removing SSE helps on HiTab.

The correlation analysis (Sec 5.4) linking understanding scores to reasoning performance, the layout-level analysis (Fig. 3, Appendix F), and the token-efficiency analysis (Table 10) go beyond a standard benchmark table and add genuine insight.
Limitations are candidly discussed, including the added inference tokens of Table-GLS and reliance on decoupled structure-content data.
weaknesses: Overclaiming of consistency: the claim that DISCO 'consistently enhances table understanding across all evaluated LVLMs and tasks' is not supported by the results. Qwen3-VL-4B drops on TSD (None 28.70 -> DISCO 21.70) and OOD TCE (42.00 -> 20.00); LLaVA-v1.6-7B drops on TCE (10.72 -> 8.30); Gemma3n-E4B DA reasoning on WTQ drops after DISCO (30.50 -> 24.56). The narrative should be tempered to match the mixed results, especially for smaller models.

Potential train/test source overlap is insufficiently addressed: the DISCO alignment data (Table 5) is drawn from WTQ, HiTab, TAT-QA, TabFact, and InfoTabs — the same source datasets used for in-domain reasoning evaluation. Even if table instances differ, the paper needs an explicit statement of split discipline and ideally a leakage analysis before claims about 'internalizing the universal logic of tabular organization' can be fully credited.

Originality is modest. Structure alignment is a rule-based anonymization of existing MMTab annotations, and content alignment is template-based cell lookup; Table-GLS is a three-stage prompting pipeline (plan -> extract -> answer) similar in spirit to existing decomposition/self-verification prompting. The contribution is solid engineering and a good empirical study, but the methodological novelty is limited for a main-track paper.

No statistical significance testing, error bars, or variance estimates are reported anywhere, despite a 250-sample OOD evaluation set where fluctuations of a few points (common in the tables) may not be meaningful.

The case study (Figure 5) contains internal inconsistencies that undermine confidence: in the Qwen3-VL + Table-GLS panel, the extracted sub-table reads 'Row 5 Column 3: W 17-10' yet the accompanying reasoning quotes 'W 35-17' and answers 18 — the evidence and reasoning contradict each other within the same example. This suggests the figure was assembled carelessly at best.

Reproducibility gaps: footnote 1 states 'Our data and code are available at' with no URL; Table 10's caption is a copy-paste error ('statistics of the scale and complexity of tables'); and there are numerous typos throughout (e.g., 'Dection', 'DiSCo' vs 'DISCO' inconsistency, 'exist methods', 'table structures' grammar). These individually are minor but collectively indicate insufficient polish.

Cross-paper comparisons in Table 3 mix models trained with different bases, data (82K-55.2K), and objectives (SFT/GRPO/preference optimization), and some numbers are quoted from original papers; the 'matches or even surpasses optimized LVLM' claim rests on these heterogeneous comparisons and should be caveated more carefully.

The 'lightweight/no tools' framing is partially offset by the token analysis: Table-GLS roughly doubles generated tokens (439 vs 241 average), a cost the paper only acknowledges in the limitations rather than reflecting in the efficiency claims of the abstract and Figure 1.

strengths: The central idea—disentangling structural abstraction (anonymized HTML/Markdown/LaTeX with placeholders) from semantic grounding (global and local content descriptions) during alignment—is well-motivated and clearly articulated, and the motivation for structure-aware, global-to-local inference without external tools is convincing.

Comprehensive evaluation across 21 tasks/benchmarks and multiple LVLM families and scales (Gemma3-12B, Gemma3n-E4B, LLaVA-v1.6-7B, Qwen3-VL-4B/8B/32B), with an appropriate data-controlled comparison (Textual 10K vs. Textual-All 97K) that supports the data-efficiency claim of matching or exceeding full-scale alignment with 10K images.

Extensive ablation and analysis: component removal (structure vs. local content alignment), Table-GLS stage removal (-GSE, -SSE), comparison to CoT and RoT, prompt-sensitivity tests (rephrase/prefix), inference-cost comparison against REFOCUS/HIPPO (Table 8), token-efficiency analysis (Table 15), non-tabular task evaluation showing no general-capability regression (Table 5), and layout/complexity analysis (Figure 3, Table 13).
The paper is transparent about limitations (dependence on decoupled data, extra token generation from multi-stage reasoning, table-only scope), which is honest and appropriate.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: data construction details, full prompts for all three Table-GLS stages (Appendix C), hyperparameters (Table 12), dataset statistics (Tables 9-11), and a stated code/data release.
weaknesses: Results are mixed in places and the claims sometimes overstate the evidence: on Qwen3-VL-4B, DISCO substantially degrades TSD (36.60 -> 21.70) and OOD TCE Row (44.40 -> 20.00) versus the Textual baseline; on reasoning, HIPPO still achieves a higher average (64.58) than the best Qwen3-VL-8B-DISCO result (59.48), so 'comparable to optimized LVLM' is only partially supported.

The headline case study (Figure 5) contains internally inconsistent content: the non-DISCO Table-GLS branch shows sub-table 'Row 5 Column 3: W 17-10' but the reasoning text quotes 'W 35-17', and the DISCO branch's correct answer (7) is derived from a sub-table reading that conflicts with the CoT branch's reading of the same cell. This undermines confidence in the qualitative evidence and suggests possible errors in presentation or data handling.

No statistical significance testing, variance across seeds, or confidence intervals are reported anywhere, despite many near-threshold comparisons (e.g., several Table 2/6/7 ablations differ by ~1-2 points); the human study on the revise mechanism uses only 50 instances and 4 annotators with no inter-annotator agreement reported.

Novelty is moderate: structure/content disentanglement reduces to a fairly straightforward data-construction recipe (anonymized serialization targets plus cell-level QA), and Table-GLS is a plan-then-extract prompting pipeline conceptually close to ReFocus and CoT-style decomposition; the paper could better quantify what is new relative to these inference-time baselines beyond latency.

Writing quality issues undermine polish: repeated misspellings ('dection', 'statitiscs', 'Contruction', 'evaluate', 'structure' typos), Table 15's caption is wrong (it repeats the caption of Table 13 instead of describing token statistics), and equation/instruction notation is described loosely rather than precisely.

The Table-GLS pipeline roughly doubles tokens versus CoT (Table 15: 454 vs. 252 average) and requires three sequential LVLM calls; the 'lightweight/efficient' framing in the abstract and introduction is somewhat in tension with this cost, which is only discussed in the limitations and Appendix G.

Small-model results (Gemma3n-E4B, LLaVA-v1.6-7B) are weak in absolute terms, indicating the gains may depend heavily on strong base models, which limits the generality of the 'transfers intrinsic reasoning' claim.

strengths: The evaluation is unusually broad for this area: 21 table understanding and reasoning benchmarks across four LVLM backbones of different scales (Gemma3-12B, Gemma3n-E4B, LLaVA-v1.6-7B, Qwen3-VL-4B/8B/32B), with out-of-domain settings and multiple closed/open-source baselines.

The core motivation is sensible and clearly articulated: decoupling structural perception from semantic grounding during alignment is an intuitive design principle, and the ablations (structure-only, w/o local content alignment) empirically probe each component (Tables 1, 14).

The analysis sections go beyond headline numbers: prompt-sensitivity tests (Table 6), a revise-mechanism ablation (Table 7), token-cost analysis (Table 15), non-tabular transfer evaluation (Table 5), and a layout/complexity breakdown (Table 13, Fig. 3/6) all strengthen the empirical picture.
The limitations section is honest and specific (dependence on decoupled supervision, added inference latency, table-only scope), which is appreciated.
The data-efficiency framing (10K images vs. 97K/150K for textual alignment) is a practically useful observation if it holds.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. DISCO reduces to (a) SFT on anonymized-structure supervision and (b) SFT on cell-lookup/global-description supervision; both are simple supervised alignment tasks closely related to Table-LLaVA's cell-level alignment. Table-GLS is a three-stage prompting pipeline (plan rows/columns, verify plan, extract sub-table, then answer) that is very close to existing plan-and-extract and attention-steering methods such as ReFocus, differing mainly in being prompt-only. Neither component involves new modeling or learning machinery.

The central 'efficiency' claim is partially contradicted by the paper's own numbers. Table-GLS generates ~2x the tokens of CoT on average (512.89 vs 251.62, Table 15), and Table 8 shows 12–15 s per sample versus 0.72–0.86 s for HIPPO — roughly 15–20x slower. The claim of a 'better balance' than tool-augmented methods is defensible, but the abstract's efficiency framing is overdrawn.

Results are mixed in ways the narrative does not fully confront. DISCO degrades direct answering on WTQ for Gemma3n-E4B (30.50 → 24.56), and on Qwen3-VL-4B TSD drops sharply (28.70 → 21.70) while OOD TCE falls from 42.00 to 20.00. In Table 2, removing SSE improves HiTab (31.41 vs Full 27.35), and 'only Table-GLS' beats Full on InfoTabs (73.59 vs 72.67). These inconsistencies deserve deeper analysis rather than selective emphasis.

The case study (Figure 5) contains internal contradictions that undermine its evidentiary value: the extracted sub-table reads 'Row 5 Column 3: W 17–10' while the accompanying reasoning quotes 'W 35–17'; the middle panel (Qwen3-VL + Table-GLS) produces the wrong answer 18 while the main text asserts Table-GLS 'successfully localizes the relevant row and result cell'; and a correct answer of 7 is derived from a wrong sub-table value.

The revision-reliability study is too small and loosely reported to support claims: 50 instances, 4 raters, per-rater percentages (78%, 80%, 76%, 72%) with no inter-annotator agreement, no protocol description, and no aggregated confidence interval.

Reproducibility is compromised: the abstract's code and data link is literally blank ('available at .'), which for a paper whose value rests on prompting details and data construction is a significant gap. The prompt appendix helps, but the pipeline's parsing/fallback behavior is not described.

Potential train/test overlap is not clearly addressed. The DISCO alignment data (Table 9) is sampled from sources including WTQ, HiTab, TAT-QA, TabFact, and InfoTabs — which are also evaluation benchmarks. The paper distinguishes in-domain vs. OOD, but never quantifies whether specific table images appear in both the 10K alignment sample and the test sets, which is essential for the generalization claims.

Baseline comparisons are weakened by incomparable sources: Table-R1 (Qwen2-VL-7B) and HIPPO (MiniCPM-V-2.6) numbers are imported from their papers onto different base models, so 'comparable or superior to optimized LVLM' conclusions are not apples-to-apples. No statistical significance tests or error bars are reported anywhere.

Presentation issues reduce confidence: inconsistent naming (DISCO/DiSCo), typos ('strucuture', 'dection'), a dangling reference ('As shown in Figure, Table-GLS...' on p.4), and Table 15's caption is copy-pasted from Table 13 ('scale and complexity of tables') though it reports token counts. Table 1 header row misaligns OOD columns. Minor individually, but collectively careless.

The 'correlation' analysis (Section 5.4) is anecdotal: eight benchmark-level points across methods with no formal correlation measure or control for task difficulty, yet strong causal language ('robust table understanding forms a critical foundation').

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 21 tasks spanning table understanding (TSD, TCL, RCE, MCD, TCE with OOD splits) and reasoning (WTQ, HiTab, TAT-QA, TabFact, InfoTabs, etc.), across four LVLM families (Gemma3, Gemma3n, LLaVA-v1.6, Qwen3-VL at 4B/8B/32B) plus a closed-source model, which supports the generality claims reasonably well.

The data-efficiency comparison is well designed: DISCO (10K images) is compared against textual alignment on the same 10K images and on the full 97K MMTab alignment set, providing a controlled and fair baseline, and Table 14 adds a data-scale study (5K-20K).

Ablations are reasonably thorough: removal of GSE/SSE stages, local content alignment (w/o T_L), CoT and RoT comparisons, prompt-sensitivity variants (rephrase/prefix), a revise-mechanism analysis with a small human study, non-tabular benchmark evaluation showing no degradation of general capabilities, and token/inference-cost analysis (Tables 5-8, 15).

The core idea of disentangling structural abstraction (anonymized structure targets) from content grounding (global/local cell-level supervision) is intuitive, cheap to implement, and the evaluation of OOD/unseen table layouts is a meaningful angle.
An honest limitations section is included, covering dependence on decoupled data, added inference latency of multi-stage reasoning, and the table-centric scope.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: DISCO amounts to anonymizing cell contents in standard HTML/Markdown/LaTeX targets plus cell-lookup supervision, and Table-GLS is a prompt-based plan-then-extract-then-answer pipeline; both are natural combinations of existing ideas (MMTab-style alignment, ReFocus-style region focusing, RoT, self-refinement). The conceptual contribution is more of a well-executed recipe than a new insight.

The case study (Figure 5) contains internal inconsistencies that undermine its evidential value: in the 'Qwen3-VL + Table-GLS' branch the extracted sub-table reads 'Row 5 Column 3: W 17-10' yet the reasoning quotes 'W 35-17' and computes 35-17=18, while the DISCO branch uses the same 'W 17-10' sub-table to produce 7, matching the stated ground truth even though the sample table itself shows 'W 35-17'. This apparent editing/fabrication of illustrative outputs is a serious presentation-integrity concern.

Claims of consistent improvement are overstated relative to the numbers: e.g., Table 1 shows DISCO hurting Qwen3-VL-4B on TSD (28.70 to 21.70) and OOD TCE Row (44.40 to 20.00), and Table 3 shows Table-GLS degrading HiTab (35.47 to 27.35) and TabMCQ on Qwen3-VL-8B; the text itself states that removing SSE 'slightly improves performance on HiTab' while simultaneously claiming performance 'consistently drops' when either stage is removed.

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds for any comparison; many reported margins are small (e.g., sub-point differences in Table 5), so several conclusions may not be robust.

The headline efficiency claim is partly undercut: Table-GLS uses ~454-513 tokens and ~12-15s per sample versus direct answering, and HIPPO (trained with 55.2K images) achieves a higher average than the 8B combined method (64.58 vs 59.48), with the advantage only emerging at the 32B scale (71.84).

The human evaluation of the revision mechanism is thin: 50 instances judged by 4 undergraduates with per-judge percentages (72-80%), no inter-annotator agreement, no judging protocol, and no error bars.

Presentation quality is below the bar in places: the code URL in the abstract is empty ('available at .'), numerous typos ('strucuture', 'dection', 'exist methods', 'Table-GLS (Table-GLS)' mislabels), and the caption of Table 15 wrongly says 'statistics of the scale and complexity of tables'.

The relative contribution of DISCO vs. Table-GLS on reasoning is confounded in places: for Gemma3n-E4B, DISCO actually hurts direct answering on WTQ (30.50 to 24.56) and the Table-GLS gains largely recover this, making the average-gain narrative less clean than presented.
